title: Developing a Career Path
subtitle: Keep learning, practicing, and choosing your next edge
summary: Pip’s trusted technology no longer answers every bookshop problem. A sustainable learning habit broadens the options without chasing every novelty. A personal radar, selected experiments, and people outside the usual circle help turn curiosity into practiced judgment.

concepts.title: Continuous Breadth
concepts.body: Pip discovers that a new capability changes the shop’s deployment options. One technology’s long-term value cannot support an entire architectural career. A living set of technical and business resources plus regular exploration builds breadth while retaining useful depth. Pip asks colleagues what is worth investigating before an urgent project forces the choice.

concepts.title: The 20-Minute Rule
concepts.body: Pip reserves twenty minutes after morning coffee and before email. The chapter’s small daily commitment protects learning from the requests that displace lunch or evening plans. Pip explores an unfamiliar term and records a short note. Repeated practice turns buzzwords into topics worth deeper assessment instead of a growing list of unexplained names.

concepts.title: Build a Personal Radar
concepts.body: Pip places a new database in assess rather than declaring it production-ready. A personal radar can organize tools, languages and frameworks, techniques, and platforms. Hold avoids new use, assess investigates, trial experiments at low risk, and adopt supports trusted regular use. Pip makes portfolio decisions explicit and revisits them through reflection.

concepts.title: Diversify the Portfolio
concepts.body: Pip balances a dependable platform skill with a selected open-source contribution. The portfolio analogy weighs interestingness, employability, organizational value, and learning cost. Deliberate diversity creates options without chasing every fashionable tool or calling each experiment ready for production. Pip uses hold to protect attention from low-value information too.

concepts.title: Weak Links and Practice
concepts.body: Pip learns a new approach from someone outside the usual team. Weak links introduce perspectives and opportunities that strong links often reinforce rather than expand. Deliberate following can feed the assess queue, but learning still needs practice. Pip uses katas to explain choices and consequences under changing constraints, not collect a supposedly correct diagram.

misconceptions.claim: A career plan should specialize in one technology and wait for formal training time.
misconceptions.correction: Technology changes and formal time is easily displaced. A small daily breadth habit plus deliberate depth and practice builds a more resilient path.

misconceptions.claim: The adopt ring means a technology is universally correct and needs no further thought.
misconceptions.correction: A personal radar expresses a current portfolio judgment. Rings organize investigation and commitment; choices still depend on context and should be revisited as forces change.

scenario.title: Place the new platform on your radar
scenario.context: Your team hears strong claims about a new platform. It might improve an upcoming project, but nobody has operated it, and the organization already depends on a reliable platform that is widely supported. You have twenty minutes a day for learning and one low-risk experiment available this quarter. Decide how to investigate without letting excitement become a production commitment.

options.label: Adopt immediately
options.benefit: The team gets early experience and may gain a strategic advantage from the new capability.
options.cost: Unknown operational fit and support risk become part of a real project before evidence exists.
options.consequence: The team discovers hidden constraints under delivery pressure. Reversing the choice becomes expensive, and the radar no longer distinguishes enthusiasm from confidence.

options.label: Assess then trial
options.benefit: A short research block and bounded spike create evidence before a wider commitment.
options.cost: The team spends time learning and may conclude the platform offers no useful advantage yet.
options.consequence: The platform remains an explicit assess or trial item with notes about fit, cost, and support. The existing platform stays available while the portfolio decision matures.

scenario.debrief: A radar is a thinking scaffold, not a prediction machine. Staged commitment protects the current system while creating a deliberate path from unfamiliar idea to evidence-backed adoption.

quiz.question: When is the 20-minute rule most likely to survive the workday?
options: First thing after coffee and before checking email
Only during lunch when meetings permit
After all incoming work is finished
quiz.explanation: The chapter recommends protecting the first quiet block because lunch, evenings, and the end of the day are easily consumed by changing demands.

quiz.question: A technology has promise but you have not investigated it yourself. Which personal radar ring fits?
quiz.explanation: Assess is a staging area for research. Adopt represents trusted practice; hold is for avoiding new use or breaking a habit.

quiz.question: What makes an architecture kata valuable?
options: Repeated practice explaining trade-offs and why a design fits its constraints
Memorizing one official topology as the answer
Avoiding decisions until every uncertainty disappears
quiz.explanation: Architecture has trade-offs rather than universally right answers. Katas build design judgment by practicing decisions and rationale.

exercise.title: Create a personal radar
exercise.prompt: Choose five technologies, techniques, or habits. Place each in a quadrant and ring, schedule a 20-minute learning action, and define the evidence required to move one item to trial or adopt.
